title: Hard exam 7
about: Ten single-choice questions with traps: what a child inherits and what it cannot give back, `shift` and comments, tildes in quotes, the order of redirections in a cron line and a directory that can be read but not entered.

questions.title: What a child gives back
questions.text:
What do these lines print?
```
A=1; export B=2
bash -c 'echo $A $B; B=3; export C=4'
echo $A $B $C
```

options.why: A child process cannot change the variables of its parent.
Neither the new value of `B` nor the variable `C` travel back to the parent.
The child sees only the exported `B`; its changes are lost when it ends, and `C` never exists in the parent.
`A` was not exported, so the child does not see it.

questions.title: shift and a comment
questions.text:
`s.sh` contains:
```
echo $# $1
shift 2
echo $# $1 x#y # end
```
What does `bash s.sh a b c d` print?

options.why: The text after a `#` that starts a word is a comment, so ` # end` is not printed.
`shift 2` removes two arguments, not one.
`shift 2` drops `a` and `b`; `x#y` is one word because the `#` does not start it, and `# end` is a comment.
A `#` inside a word is just a character.

questions.title: A tilde in quotes
questions.text: A student types `cd "~/docs"`, with `docs` existing in the home directory, and gets `No such file or directory`. What is wrong?

options.t: `cd` cannot take a path that starts with a tilde, whether it is quoted or not.
options.why: `cd ~/docs` without quotes works.

options.t: The directory `docs` must always be given as `./docs` and not by its home path.
options.why: The problem is not the name but the quotes.

options.t: Quotes stop the `~` expansion, so `cd` looks for a directory named `~`.
options.why: Without the quotes, or with `"$HOME/docs"`, it works.

options.t: Double quotes make `cd` look in `/` instead of in the current working directory.
options.why: Quotes do not change where relative paths start.

questions.title: The order in a cron line
questions.text: Which `crontab` line runs `/opt/cleanup.sh` every day at 05:45 and appends both what it prints and its errors to `/var/log/cleanup.out`?

options.why: `>` replaces the log each time, and the errors are not sent to the file.
The first field is the minute and the second the hour; `45` is not a valid hour.
The order matters: `2>&1` first points the errors to where stdout was, which is not the file yet.
Minute 45, hour 5; the output is appended and then the errors follow it into the same file.

questions.title: The dot at the front of the PATH
questions.text: `PATH` is `.:/usr/bin:/bin`. The current directory contains an executable script called `ls` that prints `fake`. What does typing `ls` run?

options.t: The real `/usr/bin/ls`, because commands are always searched in `/usr/bin` first.
options.why: The directories are searched in the order of the `PATH`.

options.t: The script in the current directory, which prints `fake`.
options.why: The first directory of the `PATH` is the current one, so the local file wins; this is why `.` is dangerous there.

options.t: An error, because two commands have the same name.
options.why: The shell takes the first match and does not complain.

options.t: The script only runs if it is written as `./ls`.
options.why: That is needed only when `.` is not in the `PATH`.

questions.title: Zero or more vowels
questions.text: `w` contains the lines `bt`, `bat`, `boot`, `bit5` and `bxt`. What does `grep -c '^b[aeiou]*t$' w` print?

options.why: Only lines made of `b`, vowels and a final `t` match.
That is the count without the `$`, which also lets `bit5` in.
`bt` (no vowels), `bat` and `boot` match; `bit5` has a trailing `5` and `bxt` has a non-vowel.
`bt` also matches, because `*` allows zero vowels.

questions.title: Reading and writing the same file
questions.text:
What does the last command print?
```
echo 1 > f
echo 2 >> f
echo 3 > g
cat f g > f
cat f
```

options.why: The shell truncates `f` before `cat` runs.
`cat` reads `f` after it has been emptied, so its old lines are gone.
`>` does not append, and the original content is lost.
`> f` empties the file first, so `cat` finds `f` empty and copies only `g`.

questions.title: Comments on shutdown lines
questions.text: Which of these `shutdown` lines carries a comment that is WRONG about what the command does?

options.t: `shutdown -h +3   # halts the system after waiting three minutes`
options.why: True: `-h` halts and `+3` is the delay in minutes.

options.t: `shutdown -r 15:20   # reboots the machine when the clock says 15:20`
options.why: True: a clock time is also accepted.

options.t: `shutdown -c   # cancels a shutdown that was scheduled earlier on`
options.why: True.

options.t: `shutdown -h now   # sends SIGKILL to all processes, with no SIGTERM first`
options.why: The processes first receive SIGTERM; SIGKILL goes only to those still alive after about 5 seconds.

questions.title: Line number five
questions.text: `n` contains the numbers 1 to 8, one per line. Which command prints only the fifth line?

options.why: The last five lines start at 4, so this prints 4.
The first line alone has nothing to give to `tail -n 5`; this prints 1.
It prints from line 5 to the end: 5, 6, 7 and 8.
`head` keeps lines 1 to 5 and `tail` keeps the last of them.

questions.title: A directory you can read but not enter
questions.text: `dd` is a directory of `ana` with mode `r--r--r--` and contains the file `x`. `ana` runs `ls dd`, `ls -l dd` and `cd dd`. Which statement is TRUE?

options.t: All three work, because ana owns the directory and can read it.
options.why: Reading is not enough to cross it.

options.t: `ls dd` fails with `Permission denied`, because without `x` nothing in the directory is accessible.
options.why: Listing the names needs only `r`.

options.t: `ls dd` shows `x`, `ls -l dd` complains that it cannot access `dd/x`, and `cd dd` fails.
options.why: `r` allows the names; the details of each entry and entering need `x`.

options.t: `ls dd` and `ls -l dd` both work, and only `cd dd` fails.
options.why: `-l` has to read the attributes of the entries, which requires `x` on the directory.
